title: The simple future
topic: forming and using the future tense
why: After ir a + infinitive, seen from the very basics, the lesson introduces the simple future, which is built on the infinitive, with its ten irregular verbs (tendré, haré, diré…) and its typically Spanish use for guesses (estará en casa). It opens the unit "Plans and politeness" and provides the stem that the conditional will reuse in the next lesson.

The future: infinitive + an ending

Good news: the Spanish future is easy to build. Where English adds \"will\" in front of the verb, Spanish keeps the whole infinitive and adds an ending to it (hablar + é = I will speak). And the endings are the same for all three verb groups!

hablarcomervivir
yohablarécomeréviviré
túhablaráscomerásvivirás
él, ella, ustedhablarácomerávivirá
nosotros, nosotrashablaremoscomeremosviviremos
vosotros, vosotrashablaréiscomeréisviviréis
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablaráncomeránvivirán

Every form has a written accent except the nosotros form (hablaremos). Easy landmarks: -é for \"I will,\" -á for \"he / she will,\" -án for \"they will.\" And the endings sound like the present of the verb haber (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) glued onto the infinitive.

Reflexive verbs keep their pronoun in front: Me levantaré temprano (I'll get up early). Stem-changing verbs don't change at all, since you start from the infinitive: volveré, dormiré, pediré, empezaré.

El año que viene viviré en Sevilla y trabajaré en un hotel.Next year, I'll live in Seville and work in a hotel.
¿Cenaréis con nosotros el sábado?Will you (all) have dinner with us on Saturday?

Irregular verbs: same endings, different stem

About ten very common verbs change their stem but keep the normal endings. They fall into three families:

FamilyInfinitiveFuture (yo)English
the e of the infinitive drops outpoderpodréI'll be able to
sabersabréI'll know
quererquerréI'll want
haber (hay)habráthere will be
a d replaces the voweltenertendréI'll have
salirsaldréI'll go out, I'll leave
venirvendréI'll come
ponerpondréI'll put
two one-offshacerharéI'll do, I'll make
decirdiréI'll say

Why the d? Try saying \"tenré\" quickly: the n and r clash, so Spanish slips a d in between to smooth it out: vendré, tendré. Just like diré, they're shorter than the infinitive, not longer.

tenerhacerdecir
yotendréharédiré
tútendrásharásdirás
él, ella, ustedtendráharádirá
nosotros, nosotrastendremosharemosdiremos
vosotros, vosotrastendréisharéisdiréis
ellos, ellas, ustedestendránharándirán

Hay becomes habrá, always singular, even with a plural noun (\"there will be\"): Mañana habrá mucha gente (never \"habrán\"). And querré is spelled with two r's.

", "

When to use the future

UseExampleTranslation
distant or less certain planAlgún día viviré en la costa.Someday, I'll live on the coast.
prediction, weatherMañana lloverá en el norte.Tomorrow it will rain in the north.
promiseTe llamaré esta noche, te lo prometo.I'll call you tonight, I promise.
guess about the present—¿Dónde está Ana? —Estará en casa.— Where's Ana? — She must be at home.

The future of guessing

Here's a use that English only has in a few phrases (\"that'll be the mailman\"): Spanish uses the future all the time to make a guess about right now. Estará en casa = \"she's probably at home.\" ¿Qué hora será? = \"I wonder what time it is.\" Tendrá unos cuarenta años = \"he must be about forty.\"

Future or ir a + infinitive?

In everyday speech in Spain, for a near, decided plan, people prefer ir a: Esta tarde voy a estudiar. The simple future sounds more distant, less certain or more solemn (promises, forecasts, resolutions). It's a bit like the difference between \"I'm going to leave\" and \"I shall leave.\"

Si + present, then the future

Just like in English, never use the future after si (if): use the present, and put the future in the other half of the sentence.

Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa.If it rains, we'll stay home.

Useful time markers: mañana, pasado mañana, el año que viene, dentro de dos años, algún día, pronto, en el futuro, seguramente.
